frase_gancho.texto: Signs set in a row that still no one can read in full.

puente_narrativo.texto: Continue your route: keep exploring the spaces of the Main Plaza.

guion_corto.texto: Xochicalco had writing, and it still cannot be read in full. Helmke and Nielsen place it between the years six hundred eighty and one thousand, in the same period as the writing of Cacaxtla, Teotenango, El Cerrito and Acatlán. On the Pirámide de las Serpientes Emplumadas there is a linear text, that is, signs set in a row. The first texts from the site were published in eighteen ninety, by Peñafiel. An encyclopedia also describes a mix of Nahua-type day signs inside Maya-style cartouches, with numerals similar to Zapotec ones. That mix shows a city open to many regions. No reading is definitive. If you see signs on the building, think of it as a writing system that is still waiting for the person who will decipher it.

guion_largo.texto:
Writing is not exclusive to a single culture. In Xochicalco, people wrote too.

Helmke and Nielsen, who have studied these signs, place the city's hieroglyphic writing between the years six hundred eighty and one thousand. It was the Epiclassic period, and other cities in central Mexico were also writing: Cacaxtla, Teotenango, El Cerrito and Acatlán.

On the Pirámide de las Serpientes Emplumadas there is a linear text, that is, signs set in a row. Among them appears the date nine reed, which these specialists link to the commemoration of a New Fire ceremony.

The first texts from Xochicalco were published in eighteen ninety, by Peñafiel. Later, Caso and Berlo worked on them. Even so, the writing has not been deciphered.

The encyclopedia World History describes something curious. It says that the day signs are Nahua in type, that they sit inside Maya-style cartouches, and that the numbers resemble Zapotec ones. It is a description from a single source, but it fits what is known about the city: a place open to many regions. There is another clue: Sáenz found in an offering chamber a slab with two Nahua glyphs and two Zapotec ones.

That is why this writing is hard to read. It does not belong entirely to any known tradition. It blends resources from several, and those who made it seemed to be creating a visual language of their own for a city of diverse people.

An undeciphered writing is not a silent writing. Dates and some signs can be recognized. What is missing is the syntax, that is, how the signs are ordered to form sentences.

If you look at the building, search for the rows of signs. It may be the closest thing we have to a voice from this city.

texto.pregunta: Myth: The glyphs of Xochicalco can already be read as continuous text.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Dates and some signs have been identified, but the writing has not been deciphered.
